notes: Maxwell, 11/19/2026: a larger ERV so the bathrooms need no fans of their own. This one unit does all the bath exhaust; the two shower fans, their ducts and their wall hoods are gone. Alternatives: Panasonic Intelli-Balance 200 (about $2,730 to $3,135), RenewAire EV Premium L (30 to 280 CFM).
Dimensions are approximate: the maker's spec sheet was not reachable, so the size comes from the product class.

What to expect: an ERV core hands some moisture back to the incoming air, so it clears a steamy mirror slower than a fan blowing straight outdoors, and boost pulls from all three bathrooms at once. If the bath 1 wet room proves too steamy, a fan on its own duct to the east wall can still be added there. The unit has to run all the time so damp air does not sit in the ducts. The port layout is ASSUMED from the side port model; check Broan's drawing before hanging it.

The bathrooms exhaust through this unit instead of separate fans (Maxwell, 11/17/2026). The code allows it because the ERV sends that air outdoors; it has to run continuously at 20 CFM or more per bathroom (Ohio 4101:8-15-01, table 1505.4.4), so no bath fan is required.

Fresh air goes into the supply plenum, not the attic (Maxwell, 11/18/2026). ERV makers' instructions say the furnace blower should run whenever the ERV runs when it is tied into the ductwork, and Building Science Corp. calls for an interlock and a motorized damper on a supply side connection. The heat pump's ECM blower can idle at low speed for this. Andy should confirm the ERV can push against the supply plenum's pressure; the fallback is the return plenum, which the code also counts as supply ventilation (IRC M1505.4.1).

One fan pulls from all three bathrooms, so the whole exhaust duct is under suction and air cannot be pushed from one bathroom into another. Backdraft dampers are for separate fans that share a duct. Each branch gets a balancing damper to set its airflow.

Set out to the Panasonic installation instructions the first unit came with (Maxwell, 11/18/2026); check them against Broan's: the two outdoor hoods are more than 10 ft apart, every duct connection has 2 ft or more of straight run before its first elbow, the outdoor ducts are insulated, the unit hangs level on chains inside the conditioned attic, and the intake is well over 6 ft from the dryer and range hood outlets.

A backdraft damper in the fresh air duct stops the heat pump's blower from pushing supply air backward through the ERV. With the blower off, the ERV's own fan still sends the fresh air down the supply trunk to every register, so it works without the heat pump running. Whole house ventilation is about 75 CFM for this size and bedroom count, and a full boost is about 190 CFM, inside this unit's 210. Andy should confirm the size. The range hood cannot connect here, it has its own duct outdoors.

Litter box exhaust (Maxwell, 11/20/2026): a fourth pickup, 20 CFM from a low grille behind the litter box in the utility room. The bath grilles keep their 20 each, so the continuous setting goes from about 65 to 80 CFM (fresh air rises with it, the unit stays balanced). A 20 CFM constant airflow regulator on that branch holds it at 20 on boost too, so boost is unchanged for the bathrooms.

The video's catch: high speed is loud because 600 CFM squeezes through a small screened grille. The big hood box around it is the fix: it holds the smoke so normal speed has time to catch it.
The fan sits inside the hood, so the duct ends at a plain wall cap outside. A remote exterior blower would be quieter on high, but it loses the heat sensor that makes the hood run on its own.

Ohio only requires makeup air over 400 CFM when a fuel burning appliance is inside, and this house is all electric. Still, this house is very tight, so on high crack the kitchen window, or add a makeup air damper later.

notes: Out the side of the house instead of through the roof (Maxwell, 11/20/2026), high on the west wall and tucked under the 12 in rake overhang, straight out from the hood.

Code check (Ohio residential code 4101:8-15-01): the roof is an unvented SIP roof with no soffit vents, so nothing can draw the exhaust back in at the eave, and 1501.1 only bars discharging INTO an attic, soffit or ridge vent; a wall opening under an overhang is fine. It is about 6 ft from the kitchen door (3 ft required from operable doors and windows), about 8-1/2 ft from the kitchen window round the corner, and about 24 ft from the ERV's outdoor air intake on the same wall (10 ft required). It blows down, away from the path to the kitchen door (303.5.2: not onto walkways).

Expect some grease film on the siding and the underside of the overhang over the years; the black trim hides it. Pick one whose louvre can be cleaned (303.6 wants 1/4 to 1/2 in openings on exhaust outlets). A cap with a fine bug screen would clog with grease.

How it helps the air: the supply comes in high at the door wall and throws along the sloped ceiling toward the window, and the returns are in the same wall. In cooling, forward (downdraft) pulls that supply air down over the chair and the computers before it comes back, and the breeze lets the thermostat sit a degree or two warmer. In heating, warm air stays up under the high side of the ceiling by the high return; the fan on low in reverse (updraft) turns the air over the whole room.

Warm air from the computers rises toward the high side, where the high return is. The fan mixes; it does not move air out of the room. The supply and returns still do that, so this is a companion to the ducts, not a fix for an undersized one.

info.model: 8 in round exhaust
notes: 8 in smooth galvanized duct from the top of the power pack, up the chimney enclosure, one elbow just under the ceiling, then straight west through the SIP wall to the wall cap under the rake overhang. 8 in, not 6 in: the video's point that a 6 in duct chokes the real airflow, and the PM600SSV only reaches its top speed on 8 in. A range hood may not connect to the ERV or the return: the Ohio residential code (1503.3) requires its own smooth, air tight metal duct to the outdoors with a backdraft damper, and never into an attic or soffit. Where it passes the wall: a galvanized sleeve through the SIP, the foam cut back and sealed with the SIP maker's sealant and tape, the hole clear of the top plate and panel splines, and the sleeve flashed into the rain screen wrap behind the siding. Insulspan should confirm the hole and its spot.
